item.title: Humble hawthorns ride a growing wave of popularity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
As tanghulu heralds the arrival of winter, craze for the fruit in its many forms only keeps increasing When winter is around the corner, can tanghulu, the traditional Chinese candied fruit snack, be far behind? The colorful snack is back on the streets and in cyberspace, creating a sweet sensation on social media by garnering millions of views. For many Chinese people, the first taste of autumn is a stick of tanghulu, sold at every corner as the weather turns cold. Mainly made of fresh hawthorn dipped in sugar syrup, the snack offers a tart contrast to traditional sweets. But tanghulu is just one of the many ways that hawthorns are savored. The fruit is eaten dried, preserved, brewed and even cooked with meat. In Xinglong county, Hebei province — known as China's hometown of hawthorn — the fruit's many edible forms are on full display. Some of the variations can surprise even seasoned foodies: black-coffee hawthorn cakes, prune hawthorn cubes, blueberry-filled hawthorn snacks, fruit leather that stretches more than half a meter, and tangerine-peel-and-red-ginseng hawthorn pills that give traditional healthy-eating ideas a modern twist. Traditionally, hawthorn is valued for helping relieve indigestion. For visitors to Xinglong, the fruit tastes different when eaten straight from the tree. "I was completely blown away. Hawthorn trees were everywhere, covering the hillsides as far as the eye could see. Almost every home had the trees right outside the front door," said Ren Qingling, a 45-year-old from Beijing, who visited Xinglong in October with her family. "The fresh fruit was much more sour than I expected. The locals told me to leave it for a while and it would taste better," she said. Chinese hawthorns are commonly grouped into two categories by region — northern and southern — according to the Kunming forestry and grassland bureau of Yunnan province. Northern hawthorns, found in Shandong and Hebei provinces, are large, bright red in color with pale spots, and have a sour taste with a hint of sweetness. Southern hawthorns, grown in parts of the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region and Zhejiang, Hubei and Yunnan provinces, are smaller, darker and more sour. In Yangzhou, Wuxi and Suzhou in Jiangsu province, cooks combine the sweet-and-sour flavors of hawthorns to make dishes such as hawthorn ribs and hawthorn meatballs. According to The Compendium of Materia Medica, a classic Chinese herbal text written by Li Shizhen in the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), hawthorns act as a softening agent when boiled with old chicken or tough meat. The range of uses depends on how the fruit is handled, and growers understand this. Chen Yikai, who runs a hillside farm in Banbishan town of Xinglong county, has already finished harvesting his produce. For him, handpicking is key. "Fruit for tanghulu must be handpicked. It must be free of cuts or scars. Intact fruit commands a higher price." Much of his crop is tieshanzha, or "iron hawthorn", a firm variety used for tanghulu and juice. "It keeps well and can last until May next year," the 53-year-old said. Chen started growing hawthorns in 2000 on about 6.7 hectares and now farms nearly 27 hectares. He initially ran the orchard as a side business while working in the transportation sector. Now, agriculture is his main business, thanks to the fruit's rising prices. "The land suits the fruit. My orchards are on high-altitude mountain land with loose soil rather than hard, heavy clay. Also, wide day-night temperature swings aid growth," he said. Wang Qiong, a researcher at the Institute of Food Science and Technology of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, told Hebnews.cn in October last year that "Xinglong has ample resources and industrial and geographical advantages, which should be fully used". "Since hawthorn is both food and medicine, we should identify its key beneficial compounds and increase the value of hawthorn products," she said. "In processing, we should use advanced technologies to develop distinctive, high-value hawthorn products and help Xinglong upgrade and transform its hawthorn industry." lihongyang@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Jan-Sept growth driven by opening-up
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
Jan-Sept growth driven by opening-up Stable expansion of manufacturing, services sectors, FDI all key reasons China's continued economic growth and further opening-up are reinforcing foreign companies' confidence in the Chinese market, encouraging them to expand their manufacturing and research activities in the country, experts and business executives said. The nation's GDP grew 4.6 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters, supported by stable growth in the manufacturing and services sectors, according to the latest data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. Yu Peng, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing, said China's growing industrial capabilities and improved market access are encouraging foreign enterprises to expand investment in high-tech manufacturing and research and development across the country. That view is in line with the latest foreign direct investment data. FDI in high-tech industries surged 33.8 percent year-on-year to 228.53 billion yuan ($34.28 billion) between January and September, accounting for 41.6 percent of the national total, said the Ministry of Commerce. Investment in China from Canada, France, Switzerland and the United States rose 90.5 percent, 31.8 percent, 26 percent and 7.7 percent on a yearly basis, respectively, during the period. Zhou Nianli, a professor at the University of International Business and Economics' Academy of China Open Economy Studies in Beijing, said China's opening-up policies, big-ticket trade events — such as the China International Import Expo — green transition and consumption upgrading are creating fresh opportunities for foreign businesses seeking long-term growth in the country. As global supply chains evolve, multinational companies are reassessing their regional strategies to balance production capacity, market proximity and operational flexibility, said Zhou. Speaking ahead of the upcoming ninth CIIE in Shanghai from Nov 5 to 10, Yin Zheng, executive vice-president of China and East Asia operations at Schneider Electric, said businesses face both challenges and opportunities as technology advances, and energy transition and industrial upgrading continue to reshape the global industrial landscape. "China's solid industrial foundation, abundant innovation resources and diverse application scenarios provide significant opportunities for collaboration," said Yin. He added that the French industrial group is working with local partners to integrate electrification, automation and digital technologies across industries, helping businesses improve efficiency and accelerate their green transition. Schneider Electric, which is set to participate in the CIIE for the ninth consecutive year, has expanded its campus in Beijing and completed construction of a new industrial park in Wuxi, Jiangsu province this year. It is preparing to launch operations at its industrial park in Xiamen, Fujian province. This will become the group's largest production base globally for medium-voltage electrical equipment. Americhem Inc, a US producer of specialty plastic compounds and additives, put a new clean compounding facility into operation in Suzhou, Jiangsu, in late September. John Richard, CEO of Americhem, said the investment will enhance the company's capacity to serve customers in China and other Asia-Pacific markets, particularly those in the healthcare sector. Meanwhile, Mike Crichton, president, international, at GSK Plc, said the British biopharma company is proud of its long-standing role in China's healthcare journey and remains committed to contributing to the Healthy China Initiative. "With our Chinese partners, we are accelerating access to innovative medicines and vaccines for hepatitis B, shingles, HIV and tuberculosis. We are especially encouraged by the focus of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) on disease prevention and healthy aging, including adult vaccination," Crichton said. zhongnan@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Tianjin's old industrial heart beats with new life
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
A group of visitors dressed as factory workers from the 1950s scurry among the cafes and landscaped paths at Jinyi Park in Hedong district, Tianjin. They collect work badges, search for technical drawings, solve riddles and try virtual machine operations as part of an immersive game at the former Tianjin No 1 Machine Tool Works. Hunting for clues in old workshops and offices, they follow routines that were once part of everyday life in the compound. Outside, visitors sit on the lawns and indulge in a variety of activities with their friends and pets. Yang Zhong, a researcher at the housing and urban-rural development commission of Hedong district, said the challenge has been to inject the old factory with a new lease on life without losing its original character. "We wanted to preserve, as much as possible, the feeling of the original factory's spatial layout," Yang said. The Tianjin factory was one of the State-owned machine tool enterprises known as the "18 Arhats", a group of key enterprises that helped develop the country's machinery industry. Established in 1951, it produced China's first all-gear transmission lathe with independent intellectual property rights. After production moved to Xiqing district, more than 20 kilometers away, the old compound eventually fell idle. A State-owned company began planning its revitalization in 2020, and the renewal project got underway in 2023. The wider project covers about 730,000 square meters, including the former factory compound of roughly 280,000 sq m and 15 surrounding residential compounds. Within the factory site, more than 20 old industrial buildings have been retained for renovation and reuse. The transformation reflects Tianjin's efforts to reinvigorate old industrial compounds while preserving their important role in the nation's development. One of China's major industrial cities, Tianjin was once home to bustling textile, machinery and light-industrial sectors. But as factories relocated or closed amid industrial restructuring, many compounds fell into disuse, opening the way for their repurposing as cultural, tourism and leisure destinations. Restoring character The Jinyi Park renewal team worked with a design institute affiliated with Tianjin University to assess buildings individually. Their age, history, former functions and preservation value were taken into consideration, Yang said. Some could be retained mostly as they were, while others needed major repairs or remodeling to make them useful again. Decades of neglect and updated fire-safety requirements added to the workload. One building required particular care. Built in 1951 to accommodate Soviet experts working at the factory, it had an exterior made of specially treated and strengthened bricks. Over the years, the exterior had been covered with pale yellow paint. Photographs from the 1970s showed that the original brickwork was red, said Lyu Hong, chief engineer of the renovation project. The team removed the yellow paint, only to find that some bricks were damaged or missing, and parts of the structure were uneven. Different methods were used to repair the facade, including replacing missing sections and applying brick pieces and brick powder. But not every damaged section was concealed. "We kept some of the bricks that were badly damaged so people could still see their original condition," Lyu said. The team also addressed uneven settlement of the structure through brickwork repairs and grouting. The walkway outside was repaired, while inside the original terrazzo floor, wooden floorboards, timber roof, staircase, railings and dado wall features were preserved or restored. When sunlight falls across the old staircase, the beauty of the terrazzo floor and wooden details that survived more than seven decades are highlighted. "The way the light changes across this space is especially moving," Lyu said. The building's old materials and changing light, she said, are part of what gave the interior its character. The renovated building opened in November 2025, with Yichi Garden cafe as a new tenant. Plants, books, lighting and furnishings have been added, but the original structural details remain. Customers can eat, read, work, cosplay or spend time with friends in rooms that once accommodated the factory's Soviet experts. "When customers enter the space and see these machines and the surroundings, they feel as if they are having a conversation with time," said cafe manager Wan Bifeng. "Former factory workers sometimes return to the compound, recognize machinery displayed downstairs and tell us that they once worked with the equipment," she said. The renewal team had to work with aspects of the industrial site that could not easily be moved or removed. "We designed the roads around the old trees rather than moving them to make way for the roads," Yang said. A former factory canteen presented a particular challenge. It had been earmarked for demolition to make way for a road planned to pass through the site. Instead, the team designed an open central space with glass curtain walls on both sides. The glass sections can be dismantled if the road eventually goes ahead, allowing the building to remain in use for now, Yang said. The team took a similar approach to the factory's equipment, incorporating overhead cranes, columns, old machines and machine parts into the renewed spaces. Museum pieces Housed in a former workshop at Jinyi Park, the Tianjin Machine Tool Industry Museum includes three machines recovered from the original factory. The team found the machines while making an inventory of the factory's fixed assets, said Li Mengyan, a museum guide. One is a straight bevel gear planer. Visitors can learn about its function through the exhibits or try operating a virtual version of it on an interactive screen, turning controls and pressing buttons to earn a score. The museum displays extend beyond machine tools to the products and institutions that shaped the city's industrial life. They include time-honored Tianjin brands such as White Rose household goods, Guifaxiang fried dough twists, Yumeijing skincare products and Sea-gull watches, alongside exhibits about local universities and newer technology companies. Together, they reflect the range of Tianjin's manufacturing and commercial history, from everyday household products and traditional snacks to skincare and watchmaking. Li said the museum plans to include more local manufacturers in its collection. The reuse of idle industrial buildings at Jinyi Park is part of Tianjin's wider urban renewal agenda. The city's special urban renewal plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, announced in May, sets out 26 key tasks and identifies 215 urban renewal areas. It calls for the revitalization of idle and inefficient factory buildings, stronger protection of industrial heritage and the development of new uses and business models. Elevated experience Before Lyu Chenghua became involved in the redevelopment of a disused textile factory in Xiqing district, weeds choked its grounds. Redbrick workshops that had stood idle for years, offered little indication of the restaurants, cafes and bars that would eventually fill the compound. Lyu, an investor in the redevelopment, had considered 13 sites for an industrial-themed project before settling on the former textile factory. He wanted something different from a conventional commercial complex. "When you develop a site in an old factory, people are drawn to the city's memories, its industrial character and the stories behind it," he said. His concept has materialized via an elevated walkway known as the Years Corridor that spans more than 200 meters, connecting 35 buildings. Visitors climb a retro-style staircase to look across a patchwork of redbrick roofs and old trees growing between buildings with the city's modern skyline in the background. The elevated route is among the site's most recognizable attractions, with designated spots for photographs and nearly 30 other interactive features aimed at younger visitors. On the restored roof of an old workshop, visitors can walk across weathered tiles. The former factory has become a place to eat, drink, shop and spend an evening out. The Tianjin Sezhi Factory tourism and leisure block opened to the public in May 2026. In its first three months of trial operation, it received about 2 million visits, according to local media reports. Average daily foot traffic exceeded 20,000 on weekdays and 30,000 on weekends and holidays, the reports said. Around 100 businesses occupy about 15,000 sq m of renovated space. They include restaurants, specialty coffee and tea shops, children's activities centers, creative retail outlets and intangible cultural heritage workshops. For Lyu's team, the challenge was to make these businesses functional without erasing the history of the original buildings. Tenants have retained original workshop layouts and industrial features in their designs. Some coffee shops have built counters over abandoned textile-machine stations, while restaurants leave steel beams and concrete walls exposed. Creative shops use old yarn spindles and weaving shuttles as display pieces. The restoration itself required considerable work. Some walls had collapsed and had to be rebuilt on their original sites, while roofs needed repair or replacement, Lyu said. Whatever you like The team has also adjusted the mix of art, culture, catering and other businesses to draw customers with different tastes. "What we're building is tourism and culture combined with consumption," Lyu said. Some restaurants serve customers until 2 or 3 am, while some bars stay open until 5 am. Where textile production once set the rhythm of the site, diners, music fans and late-night customers now keep its lights on. Tianjin Zhiwanfeng restaurant is run by Zhao Dongfang, who worked in equipment manufacturing for more than 20 years. He said he had passed the former textile factory many times without knowing much about its history. One evening in May, Zhao noticed lights at the site while driving past. He returned the next day to look around. The outdoor space and a stage caught his attention, and he decided to rent a space for a restaurant. "I like the industrial style. It makes people feel comfortable and relaxed," Zhao said. His restaurant opened in mid-July. Its indoor area covers about 300 sq m, with the outdoor section a similar size. It opens at 9:30 am, serving coffee, cold drinks and desserts during the day before shifting to dinner, drinks and live music in the evening. Three singers perform daily, according to Zhao. The restaurant usually stays open until about 2 am, although some customers remain until 4 am. Most of the evening crowd is young, he said. At Yichi Garden cafe, Wan has seen repeat and first-time customers drawn by the building's Soviet-era atmosphere. Her team has adapted the space to accommodate different usages. A room that attracted visitors wanting to take photographs proved disruptive for diners, so the team created a designated photo area downstairs, she said. Wan herself has found the quieter corners useful. "Sometimes, I retreat to a private room in the former experts' building, just to enjoy the calm atmosphere, so I can better concentrate my mind on the paperwork," she said. Contact the writers at yangfeiyue@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China rising as leader in clean governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
China rising as leader in clean governance Draft law: Need for international coordination highlighted In a move signaling its rise as a global leader in clean governance, China is preparing a landmark law to codify its overseas anti-corruption campaigns into a permanent framework covering repatriation of fugitives, recovery of illicit offshore assets and management of officials stationed abroad. Legal experts said the draft, which is being reviewed by Chinese lawmakers, clarifies the duties of departments involved in fighting cross-border corruption, and addresses the long-standing challenge of corrupt officials and businesspeople fleeing overseas or funneling illicit funds into foreign real estate and offshore bank accounts. The proposed law is also seen as a concrete move to implement the Communist Party of China's requirement for full and rigorous self-governance. Since the 18th National Congress of the CPC in 2012, there has been stricter oversight of Party conduct, the fight against corruption has intensified, and Beijing has advocated a new international anti-corruption order, pushing for new progress in international fugitive repatriation and asset recovery. President Xi Jinping, who is also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, has on multiple occasions made important remarks on international anti-corruption exchanges. In January 2016, Xi underscored at the sixth plenary session of the 18th CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection that greater efforts should be made to track down corrupt officials who have fled overseas and to recover the money they have stolen. He stressed the need to promote international cooperation under multilateral frameworks such as the G20, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, and to carry out special programs on a global scale to pursue criminals, seek out fugitives and warn those who harbor dreams of fleeing. In May 2017, when delivering a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation in Beijing, Xi called for the strengthening of international counter-corruption cooperation, so that the Belt and Road will be a road with high ethical standards. Between 2017 and 2022, "Sky Net" — China's annual cross-departmental campaign to repatriate fugitives and recover illicit assets overseas — brought back 6,900 fugitives and recovered 32.79 billion yuan ($4.9 billion) in illicit funds. In 2025, authorities filed 505 cross-border corruption cases, repatriated 963 fugitives and captured all Asia-based suspects on Interpol's 100 most-wanted Red Notice fugitives. In July 2025, Zhou Jinghua, a former businesswoman and one of the 100 most-wanted fugitives sought through Interpol at China's request, was repatriated to China from Thailand. Her return meant that all fugitives on the list who had fled to other Asian countries had been brought back to China. Zhang Lei, a law professor at Beijing Normal University, said the result shows China's reach in pursuing fugitives and recovering assets. "It reflects that China's anti-corruption efforts have no forbidden zones. No matter where corrupt elements flee, they can be tracked down and brought to justice," he said. Zhang said that fugitive repatriation and asset recovery are crucial elements of international anti-corruption cooperation, adding that achievements in this regard demonstrate the overarching progress of international anti-corruption cooperation and showcase to the international community the development of China's rule of law. Yang Chao, an associate law professor at Beijing Normal University, said that implementing the UN Convention Against Corruption and proposing the Beijing Declaration on Fighting Corruption — adopted at the APEC Ministerial Meeting in Beijing in November 2014 — demonstrate China's growing role in international anti-corruption governance. "This shift helps advance law enforcement and judicial cooperation, and reduce obstacles to cross-border cases," she said. "It also narrows the space for corrupt elements to hide overseas and transfer assets, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of China's international anti-corruption cooperation." This direction has been noted by international bodies. Ghada Waly, former executive director of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, previously commended China for adopting laws aligned with the requirements of the UN Convention Against Corruption. "I am pleased to see that China has taken important steps to further align its anti-corruption framework with UNCAC requirements," she said earlier in an interview with China Daily. She also praised China's participation in the UNCAC Implementation Review Mechanism and its engagement in policy discussions, adding that "this involvement not only shows China's commitment, but also its role and contribution in shaping international policies to combat corruption". Zhuang Deshui, deputy head of Peking University's Research Center of Public Policy, said that China's draft cross-border anti-corruption law could see greater standardization. "Domestically, it helps coordinate the responsibilities of supervisory commissions, public security organs, customs and other departments, further streamlining anti-corruption workflows and fostering a unified front, thereby improving the overall effectiveness of handling cross-border corruption cases," he said. "Externally, it vividly demonstrates the CPC's achievements in exercising self-governance." Yang Weidong, a law professor at China University of Political Science and Law, said that for over a decade, China's central leadership has prioritized advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, "which requires addressing corruption among officials at all levels, in all sectors, and both at home and abroad". Yang added that managing public officials stationed overseas — in diplomatic and foreign affairs, commerce, and State-owned enterprises — remains a more challenging issue than repatriating those who fled abroad after engaging in corruption at home. He said that the time is right for China to codify its practices in cross-border corruption enforcement. "International anti-corruption governance still faces challenges," Yang said. "Addressing them through legislation will make our efforts more effective, reflect the Party's commitment to strict self-governance, and help present China as a responsible major country."

item.title: Chinese opera hits big in small theaters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
Tradition turns intimate as audiences get a close-up look at how various styles are created, performed, and expressed, Chen Nan reports. Li Chanchan and Fan Yuyan, two young students from the National Academy of Chinese Theatre Arts in Beijing, drew a crowd in a courtyard as they demonstrated a traditional jaw-dropping feat before one unleashed a burst of fire. The flames flared and vanished in an instant, prompting gasps and applause from spectators gathered among the courtyard's gray bricks and tiled roofs. The demonstration is a signature Qinqiang Opera stage skill: fire-breathing, known for its dramatic visual impact. Other performers demonstrated the sweeping spear movements of Peking Opera, offering a glimpse of the physical precision and theatrical spectacle that has sustained traditional Chinese opera for generations. At the 13th Xiqu Opera Black Box Festival, which opened at Star Theaters in Beijing on Oct 14, tradition is also being explored through more intimate, unexpected storytelling forms. The festival runs through Nov 22 and brings together 16 productions tailored for smaller theaters spanning 11 traditional Chinese opera genres, including Peking Opera, Kunqu Opera, Yuju Opera, Pingju Opera, and Cantonese Opera. The opening performance, The Face in the Mirror, a Huaiju Opera production, takes audiences into a world of illusion and psychological unease, asking what happens when people finally obtain what they desire.

item.title: World Bank director sees China's buzzwords
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
World Bank country director: What development keywords can a robot exhibition reveal about China? Over the past four plus decades and more, China has achieved rapid development and structural transformation, lifting 800 million people out of extreme poverty, and steadily raising incomes and welfare. Citing the World Robot Conference in Beijing as an example, Tatiana Rosito, World Bank country director for China, Mongolia, and Korea, noted that robotics is accelerating on the ground in China, boosting productivity and changing people's daily lives. She said she looks forward to China's 15th Five-Year Plan, including new productive forces, high-quality development, more and better jobs, and green transition. The World Bank's cooperation with China will focus on three pillars: promoting productivity and job growth, enhancing human capital for better jobs, and strengthening resilient infrastructure and natural capital. (Reporter: Li Wei; Video: Pan Yixuan, Cheng Zixin)
